title: The ladder: senses, objects, mind, intellect, the great self
theme: Beyond the senses are their objects, beyond the objects the mind, beyond the mind the intellect, and beyond the intellect the great self.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «सूक्ष्मा महान्तश्च प्रत्यगात्मभूताश्च», subtler, greater and more inward
Śaṅkara: the subtle elements from which the senses arise, «यैः परैरर्थैरात्मप्रकाशनायारब्धानि»; Raṅgarāmānuja: the objects of the senses, «विषयाः»
Śaṅkara: the first-born Hiraṇyagarbha principle, «हैरण्यगर्भं तत्त्वं»; Raṅgarāmānuja: the individual self, called great because all depends on its will

sandhi.type: āḥ before a voiced sound; i before a vowel; aḥ before c
sandhi.rule: The visarga after ā is dropped before the voiced h and before a vowel, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि) with P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); hi becomes hy before a, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि); the visarga of arthebhyaḥ becomes ś before c, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः) with P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः).
A final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
The visarga becomes s before t, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

sandhi.type: iḥ, eḥ before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: The visarga after i and after e becomes r before a voiced consonant or a vowel (the r of the ending).

morphology.note: para agrees with each subject in turn: parāḥ (m. pl.) with arthāḥ, param (n.) with manaḥ, parā (f.) with buddhiḥ, paraḥ (m.) with ātmā. The ablatives give the term surpassed.
Nominative masculine of mahat, ‘great’. In 1.3.11 the same word, mahataḥ (ablative), names this ‘great self’ as the next step.

translation.literal: Higher than the senses indeed [are] the objects, and higher than the objects the mind; but higher than the mind the intellect, [and] higher than the intellect the great self.
translation.readable: Beyond the senses are the objects, and beyond the objects the mind; beyond the mind is the intellect, and beyond the intellect the great self.

anvaya: इन्द्रियेभ्यः अर्थाः हि पराः [सन्ति], अर्थेभ्यः च मनः परम्, मनसः तु बुद्धिः परा, बुद्धेः महान् आत्मा परः ।
syntax: Four nominal sentences of the same pattern: ablative (the lower) + para- (agreeing with the subject) + nominative (the higher). The chain continues in 1.3.11 and ends there with the Person, beyond whom there is nothing.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara reads a scale of ever subtler and more inward principles, to be traced back one by one to the inmost self: «सूक्ष्मतारतम्यक्रमेण प्रत्यगात्मतयाधिगमः कर्तव्य». Raṅgarāmānuja (with the Bhāṣyakāra he quotes) reads a scale of what most needs to be brought under control, keyed to the chariot image of 1.3.3–4: «वशीकार्यत्वाय रथादिरूपितेषु शरीरादिषु यानि येभ्यो वशीकार्यतायां प्रधानानि, तानि उच्यन्ते». Madhva reads a hierarchy of the deities presiding over each.

Śaṅkara: the first-born Hiraṇyagarbha, the cosmic intellect — «अव्यक्ताद्यत्प्रथमं जातं हैरण्यगर्भं तत्त्वं बोधाबोधात्मकं महानात्मा बुद्धेः पर इत्युच्यते». Raṅgarāmānuja: the individual self, the rider of 1.3.3, called great because all depends on its will. Madhva: Brahmā («तस्या ब्रह्मा महानात्मा»).

beginner: Death now explains, step by step, what lies beyond what. The senses are the first step. Beyond the senses are the things they reach for. Beyond those things is the mind, which wants them. Beyond the mind is the intellect, which decides. Beyond the intellect is what the verse calls the great self. Each step is higher, deeper or more important than the one before, and the list goes on in the next verse. The commentators read the ladder in different ways. Śaṅkara sees a path inward: each step is subtler than the last, and one traces them back toward the inmost self. Raṅgarāmānuja, using the chariot picture, reads it as an order of control: the objects pull harder than the senses, the mind more than the objects, and so on. Madhva reads a ladder of presiding deities.
analogy: Like following a river upstream: each stretch is fed by a higher one, until one reaches the spring.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It ranks five things: the objects stand above the senses, the mind above the objects, the intellect above the mind, and the great self above the intellect. The next verse continues the series.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: a scale of subtlety, traced inward
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The ladder is given so that the goal may be reached as one's inmost self, from the gross senses through ever subtler steps: «स्थूलान्यारभ्य सूक्ष्मतारतम्यक्रमेण प्रत्यगात्मतयाधिगमः कर्तव्य इत्येवमर्थमिदमारभ्यते». The ‘objects’ are the subtle elements from which the senses are made; ‘mind’ and ‘intellect’ name the subtle elements that produce them («भूतसूक्ष्मम्»); the great self is the first-born Hiraṇyagarbha, «हैरण्यगर्भं तत्त्वं».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He comments on 1.3.10 and 1.3.11 together («इन्द्रियेभ्यः पराः इत्यादिमन्त्रद्वयेन») and quotes the Bhāṣyakāra on the ānumānika-adhikaraṇa. The steps are ranked by how much each needs to be brought under control: the objects outrank the senses, because even one whose senses are controlled finds them hard to hold when objects are near — «वश्येन्द्रियस्यापि विषयसन्निधौ इन्द्रियाणां दुर्निग्रहत्वात्»; the mind outranks the objects; the intellect, the charioteer, outranks the mind; the self, the rider, outranks the intellect as the agent, and is called great because all depends on its will: «सर्वस्य आत्मेच्छायत्तत्वात्, आत्मैव महान् इति विशेष्यते».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: His comment, in verse, names a deity at each step. Higher than the deities of the senses are those presiding over objects: «देवेभ्य इन्द्रियात्मभ्यो ज्यायांसोऽर्थाभिमानिनः». The mind's deities are Rudra and others; above them the intellect is Sarasvatī: «ते श्रेष्ठा अर्थमानिभ्यस्तेभ्यो बुद्धिः सरस्वती». The great self is Brahmā: «तस्या ब्रह्मा महानात्मा».

commentary.q: The same words in the Gītā
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Bhagavad Gītā 3.42 gives a shorter ladder in almost the same words — the senses, the mind, the intellect, and ‘he’ beyond the intellect. The Kaṭha's version inserts the objects between the senses and the mind, and continues further in 1.3.11.

advaita.text: A scale of subtlety and inwardness by which the goal is known as one's own inmost self: «प्रत्यगात्मतयाधिगमः कर्तव्य». The great self is the first-born Hiraṇyagarbha.

visistadvaita.text: An order of what most needs control, read through the chariot image; the great self is the individual self, the rider, «आत्मैव महान् इति विशेष्यते».

dvaita.text: A hierarchy of the deities presiding over each step, the intellect being Sarasvatī and the great self Brahmā: «तस्या ब्रह्मा महानात्मा».

schools.disagreement: Whether the ladder is a path of inward tracing to the one Self (Śaṅkara), an order of control in which the great self is the individual soul (Raṅgarāmānuja), or a hierarchy of presiding deities (Madhva).

parallels.note: The Gītā's shorter ladder: senses, mind, intellect, and ‘he’ beyond the intellect.
The Brahmasūtra's ānumānika-adhikaraṇa discusses this verse and the next; the ‘unmanifest’ of 1.3.11 is taken as the body of the chariot image, not the Sāṅkhya pradhāna.

parallels.quote: मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिः — बुद्धिं ह्यारुह्य भोग्यजातं भोक्तारमुपसर्पति
parallels.note: Śaṅkara, in the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya, explains why the intellect stands above the mind: the objects of enjoyment reach the enjoyer by way of the intellect.

contemporary.text: The verse is an early map of attention: what the senses take in, what the mind wants, what the intellect decides, and who is doing all this. A map does not make the journey, but it shows where a pull is coming from — the object, the wanting, or the deciding. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Think of something that distracted you today. Was it the thing itself, the wanting of it, or the decision to follow it?
reflect.deeper: Is the ladder a map of the world, of the person, or of the way back inward? Do the three readings exclude each other?
reflect.practice: When attention is pulled away, name the step at which it happened: sense, object, mind or decision.

references.text: Raṅgarāmānuja's comment on 1.3.10 stands with his comment on 1.3.11 (edition.json maps it). In it he quotes the Bhāṣyakāra on the ānumānika-adhikaraṇa (Brahmasūtra 1.4.1); in his school the Bhāṣyakāra is Rāmānuja. The passage is reported here as quoted by Raṅgarāmānuja; Rāmānuja wrote no commentary on the Kaṭha.
Madhva's comment on 1.3.3–1.3.11 is a single passage after 1.3.11 (marked ॥ १०-१२ ॥ in the source); it concerns 1.3.10–11.

flags.note: The meaning of the ladder — inward subtlety (Śaṅkara), an order of control (Raṅgarāmānuja), presiding deities (Madhva) — and of ātmā mahān (Hiraṇyagarbha, the individual self, Brahmā).
Madhva's digital text keys अथेभ्यश्च for arthebhyaś ca, the r dropped (corrections.json, witness-error).
